summary: Mugwort is an invasive perennial plant that is widespread across North America and most common in the eastern United States and Canada. It grows along roadsides, forest edges, waste areas and lawns, and spreads aggressively through a network of underground stems (rhizomes), forming large stands of only mugwort. These stands push out native plants and can delay or disrupt the natural regrowth of plant communities. Mugwort pollen is a common cause of hay fever.
history: Mugwort is native to Europe and eastern Asia, where it has long been used as a medicinal herb. Its seed may first have been brought to North America as early as the 1500s by Jesuit missionaries in Canada. It was also spread across the continent as a contaminant in ships' ballast and in nursery stock.
seasons: Mugwort shoots come up in spring, and it flowers from July to late September with many tiny green flowers clustered at the ends of the stems. The leaves are covered underneath with woolly, silver-white hairs, and the plant has an aromatic, slightly pungent smell. The stems become somewhat woody as they age.

handling.text: Mugwort is hard to control because of its dense root system. Pulling it does not work and can even help it spread, because small pieces of root left in the soil grow into new plants (pieces as small as 2 cm can regrow). It also survives mowing, even when mowed for two years in a row. Its root pieces are easily spread when soil, yard waste and nursery plants are moved. In New York City parks like Kissena, cutting, killing or removing plants without permission from NYC Parks is against park rules, so report it instead.

report:
New York's official database for invasive species sightings is iMapInvasives, run by the New York Natural Heritage Program (a partnership between SUNY ESF and the NYS Department of Environmental Conservation). You can make a free account and report directly to the online database, which is the preferred method, or use the iMapInvasives mobile app for iPhone and Android, which can upload your records once you have a connection again. If you don't want an account, the site has a public report form; those reports are reviewed by Natural Heritage Program staff each week before being added.

In New York City parks like Kissena Park, report what you find instead of removing it yourself. NYC Parks rules forbid cutting, killing or removing any plants, flowers, shrubs or other vegetation without permission from the Parks Commissioner, and forbid chasing, harassing, harming or removing any animal, nest, or the eggs of any amphibian, reptile or bird (56 RCNY §1-04).
